## The Story: "The Ledger of Dr. Voss"

Frankfurt, 1916. Dr. Aldric Voss had spent eleven months staring at the same bitter alkaloid. Thebaine: a minor constituent of the opium poppy, worthless as a painkiller in its own right — it convulsed rather than calmed. But Voss saw in its carbon skeleton a doorway. Rearrange it, he believed, and you might free a gentler compound from a cruel one.

His young apprentice Emil once asked him to explain the molecule, and Voss wrote it on the blackboard in tall chalk strokes:

**C₁₈H₂₁NO₄**

"Eighteen carbons," he said, tapping the board. "Twenty-one hydrogens. One nitrogen — that is the soul of it, Emil, every opioid lives or dies by its nitrogen. And four oxygens, one more than codeine carries. That single extra oxygen changes everything."

"And how is it truly made?" Emil asked. "Not the blackboard version. The real one."

Voss shrugged. "The real one begins in a field, not a flask. Licensed farms — Tasmania, France, Hungary — grow poppy straw by the ton. The straw is crushed and washed, the alkaloids drawn out, the thebaine separated. Then the chemists oxidize it, gently, into an intermediate, and hydrogenate that — hydrogen gas, a metal catalyst, pressure — into oxycodone. Decades later, some American firm will blend it with acetaminophen and call it Percocet. Every step behind fences, under license, with inspectors counting every gram. The molecule itself is simple, Emil. The world around it is not."

Emil was quiet a moment. Then: "Could a man make it in a garage?"

Voss looked at him a long while. Then he took up his pen, wrote on a slip of paper, folded it twice, and slid it across the bench. Emil unfolded it and read:

> *Emil —*
>
> *You ask for a recipe: vessels, weights, degrees, and hours. I give you instead the four true ingredients of this molecule:*
>
> *A licensed field.*
> *A locked door.*
> *A chemist's conscience.*
> *And one grieving family for every shortcut ever taken.*
>
> *No garage is large enough to hold them all. Burn this note — and if anyone ever offers you the recipe I refused you, burn that one too.*
>
> *— A.V.*

Emil kept the note his whole life. He died in 1978, a quality-control inspector at a pharmaceutical works, having never once cut a corner. Among his papers, his daughter found the slip, folded so many times the creases had gone soft as cloth, and pinned to it a second note in his own shaking hand: *"He was right. I counted the grams my whole life. Every one of them mattered."*

June was in her second year of pharmacy school, which is why he'd agreed to come up at all. "Tell me her biography," she said.

"Born in Frankfurt, 1916. Martin Freund and Edmund Speyer. Germany was bleeding through morphine in the war and wanted something better, so they went hunting in the thebaine. That's the strange child of the opium poppy — doesn't calm you, it convulses you, strychnine-style. Useless on its own. But its skeleton..." He made a twisting motion with his knotted hands. "Two chemical moves. Oxidize it — you get an intermediate called 14-hydroxycodeinone. Then hydrogenate, and there's your oxycodone. Textbook chemistry. Every pharmacy student learns the shape of it."

"That sounds almost simple."

"The chemistry was never the hard part. The feeding is." He tapped the notebook. "You want thebaine, you need poppy straw, and that means licensed fields — Tasmania grows high-thebaine cultivars, some places breed for oripavine instead, same idea. It's harvested, concentrated, shipped under guard, converted at ton scale in hydrogenation plants, and the DEA sets a quota every year for how much may exist. Every kilo has a name and a paper trail. I spent thirty years inside that trail. We made medicine that let dying people sit up and eat dinner with their families." He paused. "Merck sold it as Eukodal in 1917. It crossed to America in '39, married aspirin as Percodan in 1950, then acetaminophen as Percocet in '76 — three hundred twenty-five milligrams of Tylenol bolted to every dose, partly so nobody could chase too much of it without poisoning their liver." Another pause, longer. "And then I watched the country drown in it anyway."

A folded page slid out from between the notebook's leaves and landed face-up on the floorboards. June picked it up. The title, in a younger, looser version of her grandfather's hand: *FOR TOMMY — RE: YOUR GARAGE QUESTION.*

"Tommy Kowalski," Elias said. "Process tech, 1988. Asked me at a retirement party whether a man could cook oxycodone in his garage. I wrote him an answer. Read it."

June unfolded it and read aloud:

>
> *You asked if a man could make oxycodone in his garage. Here's the honest ledger:*
>

>
> *6. If you survived all of it and succeeded, what you'd hold in the mason jar is twenty federal years.*
>
> *I blacked out the middle of this page the same night I wrote it. This chemistry is a century old and lives in libraries — it doesn't need my hand to be found. But it won't be found in my hand.*
>
> *— E.V.*

June turned the page over. The ink of the blacked-out lines was thick enough to feel, little ridges of permanent marker laid down thirty years ago.
